A grievance is a feeling — or a specific reason for that feeling — that arises when someone believes they have been treated unfairly, wrongly, or unjustly.

Think of it this way: if something happens to you that you feel was wrong, hurtful, or not fair, and it stays with you — sits in your chest like a knot — that is a grievance. It is not just a passing frustration. It carries a sense of "I was wronged, and it matters."
The Two Layers of the Word

This is the most important thing to understand: the word "grievance" works on two levels at the same time.

1. The feeling itself
This is the inner sense of injustice — the hurt, resentment, or bitterness a person carries because they feel they were treated wrongly.

"She carried a deep grievance after being passed over for the promotion."

Here, the grievance is an emotion — the wound she is holding inside.

2. The specific complaint or cause
A grievance can also refer to the actual issue — the real, concrete thing that caused the unfair treatment. In this sense, it is almost like a "case" or a "claim."

"The workers listed their grievances: low pay, dangerous conditions, and no breaks."

Here, grievances are specific complaints — things that can be listed, discussed, and (hopefully) fixed.

So in simple terms: a grievance is both the pain of being wronged AND the specific wrong that caused the pain. The two are inseparable — one feeds the other.
What Makes a Grievance Different from a Simple Complaint?

This is a key distinction. Not every complaint is a grievance.

If your coffee is cold, you might complain. That is a minor dissatisfaction.

But if you feel you were systematically underpaid for years while others doing the same job were paid more — that is a grievance. It is heavier. It involves a sense of injustice, not just inconvenience.

A grievance almost always implies:

  • A belief that something wrong was done
  • A feeling that someone (a person, institution, system, etc.) is responsible for that wrong
  • An emotional weight that lingers over time
The Emotional Quality of a Grievance

Grievances are rarely quick or light feelings. They tend to build up and stay. When someone "holds" or "harbors" a grievance, it means they are carrying that sense of injustice inside them — possibly for months or years — even without expressing it openly.

This is why grievances can be dangerous if left unaddressed. They fester. They grow. A person or a group that feels their grievances are ignored can become very resentful.
Grievances Can Be Personal or Collective

A grievance does not only belong to one person. Groups of people — workers, communities, entire nations — can share grievances.

Personal grievance:

"He had a long-standing grievance against his brother for inheriting the family business."

Collective grievance:

"The minority community had genuine grievances about how they were treated by the justice system."

When a large group of people shares a deep grievance, it can become a powerful social or political force.
Can a Grievance Be Imagined, or Does It Have to Be Real?

Both. This is a subtle but important point.

A legitimate grievance is one where the unfair treatment actually happened — it is real and verifiable.

But a person can also hold a grievance that is based on a misunderstanding, exaggeration, or even a false belief. In that case, the grievance feels completely real to the person experiencing it, even if the outside world does not see the injustice they claim.

This is why we often hear phrases like:

  • "a legitimate grievance" — to signal that the complaint is valid and justified
  • "a perceived grievance" — to suggest the injustice may not be objectively real, but the person believes it is

In workplaces and institutions, the word "grievance" takes on a more formal, almost legal meaning. When an employee believes their rights have been violated, they can formally report it. This is called filing a grievance — submitting an official complaint through a proper process so it can be reviewed and resolved.

"He filed a formal grievance with the HR department over the unfair dismissal."

In this context, a grievance is essentially a documented complaint demanding official attention.

Understanding how the word is used in common phrases will help you recognize it everywhere:

  • To nurse a grievance — to quietly hold onto a feeling of injustice over a long time, keeping it alive inside you rather than letting it go
  • To air a grievance — to openly express or voice a complaint
  • To harbor a grievance — to secretly hold a grievance, often without showing it
  • To address/resolve a grievance — to acknowledge and fix the wrong
  • A deep-seated grievance — a grievance that is old, serious, and rooted very deeply
  • A petty grievance — a small, trivial complaint that probably does not deserve as much weight as the person gives it
How Grievance Relates to Similar Words

Grievance vs. Grudge:
A grudge is purely personal and emotional — it is the ongoing resentment you feel toward a specific person. A grievance is broader and often involves a sense of injustice and a desire to have the wrong acknowledged or corrected. You can harbor a grievance and still want resolution. A grudge is more about holding onto bitterness.

Grievance vs. Resentment:
Resentment is entirely a feeling — it is the bitter, angry emotion you carry. A grievance is more structured — it includes both the feeling and the specific reason or complaint behind it. Every grievance involves resentment, but not every resentment is called a grievance.

Grievance vs. Gripe:
A gripe (informal) is a minor, everyday complaint — usually small and not deeply felt. A grievance is heavier, more serious, and implies real injustice.

If you want to remember this word in one sentence:

A grievance is the feeling — and the specific reason for the feeling — that you have been treated unjustly in a way that matters and stays with you.

It is heavier than a complaint. It carries a moral weight — "something wrong was done to me." It can be personal or shared by many. It can be expressed or quietly held inside. And if left unaddressed, it rarely disappears on its own.
